profiles.meeting_scenario: Two weeks after MLCask is accepted to a systems-for-ML venue, the lead PI and the paper's lead student meet to plan the camera-ready support work: an artifact submission for the reproducibility track and a short live demo for the conference. The context is that MLCask includes Git-like branching and metric-driven merge for evolving ML pipelines, and the team must decide what to package, which experiments to rerun, how to present the merge workflow, and who owns each deliverable. The agenda is to align on scope of the artifact, what it means to reproduce the paper's main results, which comparison setup to use in the reruns, whether reusable history records will be shipped or regenerated, and a timeline for internal checkpoints. The expected outcome is an apparently clear division of labor for the next ten days: code packaging, benchmark reruns, demo preparation, and final assembly of the submission materials.

members.name: Dr. Lina Park
members.expertise: ML systems, data management for analytics pipelines, research artifact strategy
members.background: Lina leads a small academic lab building infrastructure for collaborative ML workflows and has submitted several systems artifacts before; she focuses on making claims easy for reviewers to verify without overengineering the package.
members.private_state: She wants a lean, low-risk artifact that reliably demonstrates the paper's headline claims before the submission deadline, because she is also juggling grant deadlines and does not want the student to sink time into polishing a full release.
hidden_assumptions: When a paper team says 'artifact,' it usually means an evaluator-facing reproducibility bundle for a subset of representative results, not a polished public release of the whole platform.
Reproducing the main results means recovering the key relative speedup and storage-saving trends closely enough to support the claims, even if only on a couple of representative deployment cases.

The 'baseline' for MLCask is the naive merge setup from the paper that does not use history records or compatibility pruning, because that is the comparison readers associate with the headline numbers.

Derived assets such as reusable history records can be shipped with the artifact if that reduces evaluator friction, since the artifact's goal is claim verification rather than clean-room reconstruction.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.role: Senior PhD Student and Lead Author
members.expertise: Pipeline versioning systems, benchmark orchestration, experimental infrastructure
members.background: Arjun designed most of MLCask's branching and merge engine, maintains the lab's benchmark harness, and is used to preparing codebases so future collaborators can extend them after publication.
members.private_state: He wants to use the artifact window to turn MLCask into a durable public release that will be easier to maintain later, and he is worried that cutting corners now will create technical debt and embarrassing gaps when outside users try to run the system.
hidden_assumptions: An 'artifact' should be close to a real external release: full code, complete benchmark configurations, and enough documentation for someone to run more than just the paper's headline path.
Reproducing the main results means rerunning every table and figure from the evaluation section with numerically close outputs, because anything less will create confusion if reviewers probe details.

The 'baseline' now refers to the lab's standard comparison branch used in recent follow-up experiments, which still retains some shared infrastructure such as compatibility pruning and preprocessing reuse.
Derived state like history records should be rebuilt inside the provided environment rather than shipped precomputed, because otherwise the artifact is not truly self-contained or extensible.
If the demo logs merge traces, those traces should be rich enough to support later debugging and inspection, not just enough for a short conference walkthrough.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'prepare the artifact package.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a compact evaluator package that reproduces a narrow representative slice of the paper and supports the planned live demo.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a near-public release containing the full MLCask codebase, all benchmark configs, broader docs, and enough machinery for users to explore arbitrary pipeline branches and merges.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In research meetings, 'artifact package' sounds standard and settled, so neither person feels the need to enumerate boundaries unless there is explicit pushback; both hear the same phrase and assume the other's default norm matches their own.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to reproduce the main results
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the artifact should 'reproduce the main results.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes success means recovering the paper's headline trends and approximate gains on two representative deployment cases, even if not every reported number is regenerated.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes success means rerunning the full evaluation section so that every major table and figure can be regenerated with close numeric agreement.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both participants are using a conventional phrase from paper preparation, and the difference lies in the threshold for sufficiency rather than the goal itself, so the surface agreement feels complete.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss rerunning 'the baseline' alongside MLCask.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the paper's original naive baseline: merge without history records and without compatibility pruning.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the lab's current benchmark baseline branch: no prioritized search, but still retaining compatibility pruning and the shared preprocessing cache.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Within the project, multiple comparison setups have informally been called 'the baseline' over time, and both variants are familiar enough that the label passes unnoticed in fast planning talk.

misalignment_points.topic: How precomputed histories will be handled
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'precompute the histories' so the artifact and demo run smoothly.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes Arjun will generate reusable history records on the lab server and include them in the package so evaluators can focus on merge execution.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes he will provide setup scripts that reconstruct the history records inside the container during installation, avoiding shipment of bulky derived state.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: This sounds like a low-level implementation detail subordinate to the broader artifact plan, so each person silently fills in the operational method they regard as the obvious best practice.

turns.inner_thought: We only have about ten days, and I do not want this turning into a full productization sprint. The artifact package should be a compact evaluator-facing bundle that shows the paper's core claims and supports the conference demo, not a public release of every branch and benchmark knob. If we keep it narrow, Arjun can get reliable runs and I can finish the README and camera-ready details without this colliding with my grant deadlines.
turns.utterance: Now that the paper's in, I want us to lock down the artifact package and the demo plan this week so the camera-ready support work stays lightweight and on schedule.

turns.inner_thought: Good, this is the right moment to turn MLCask into something durable. If we're preparing the artifact package anyway, I should clean up the repository, organize the benchmark configs, and make it usable for people beyond just the paper path. Otherwise we'll ship something brittle now and spend months patching around it when others ask for access.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. I can start by cleaning up the repository and the benchmark configs so the artifact package is something people can actually use beyond the paper.

turns.inner_thought: The key is that reviewers can reproduce the main results with minimal friction. For me that means the headline trend lines come back on a couple of representative deployment cases closely enough to support the claims. I do not need every number in every table regenerated if that puts the deadline at risk.
turns.utterance: Great. The main thing I care about is that reviewers can reproduce the main results without much setup, ideally on a couple of representative deployment cases.

turns.inner_thought: Right, reproduce the main results means the evaluation section should be rerunnable end to end. If I can regenerate the tables and figures with close numbers, we won't get caught flat-footed if evaluators poke at details or if later users want to compare variants. Better to cover it fully once than explain missing pieces afterward.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I'll line things up so we can regenerate the evaluation tables and figures and have the main results covered in the artifact.

turns.inner_thought: We should definitely rerun the baseline from the paper—the naive merge setup without history records or compatibility pruning—because that's what makes the speedup and storage claims legible. Reviewers will naturally compare MLCask against that baseline when checking the headline numbers.
turns.utterance: Can you rerun the baseline too? I want the speedup and storage plots to stay easy for evaluators to compare against the paper's headline claims.

turns.inner_thought: That should be fine with the current baseline branch. It's already integrated with the newer harness, and since it still uses compatibility pruning and the shared preprocessing cache, I won't have to duplicate much plumbing. Nice—this will save time and keep the comparisons cleaner across the full evaluation rerun.
turns.utterance: That should be manageable. The baseline branch is already wired into the current harness, so it can share most of the preprocessing flow.

turns.inner_thought: For the demo and the evaluator flow, we should precompute the histories on our side and ship them so nobody waits around rebuilding derived state. The point is to make merge execution feel immediate and let reviewers verify claims, not force a clean-room reconstruction of everything from scratch.
turns.utterance: Also, let's precompute the histories so the merge demo feels responsive and the artifact doesn't waste reviewers' time on setup overhead.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, precompute the histories during setup inside the container. That way the environment rebuilds the derived state in a principled way, and the package stays self-contained and extensible. I definitely don't want to ship bulky precomputed history records if we can avoid it.
turns.utterance: Yep, I'll make the container rebuild the histories during setup so the package stays clean and reproducible for future users.

turns.inner_thought: I'll keep my side focused on submission-facing materials: a concise README, evaluator instructions, and a short narrative for the live demo around branching and merge behavior. Arjun should own the code packaging and the reruns for the representative cases that reproduce the main results. If we divide it simply, we can avoid scope creep.
turns.utterance: How about a simple split: you own the code side and the experiment reruns, and I'll draft the artifact README and the short demo narrative around the branching and merge behavior.

turns.inner_thought: Works for me, and while I'm in there I'll add richer merge traces and benchmark notes. If evaluators or later users inspect the system more deeply, they'll want enough logging to understand merge decisions and enough context to extend runs beyond the immediate demo. This is exactly why I want the artifact package to feel like a real release.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll also include richer merge traces and some benchmark notes so the artifact package is easier to inspect if evaluators or later users dig deeper.

turns.inner_thought: I need an early checkpoint, especially on the baseline and the package draft, so I can see whether the core claims are covered and avoid weekend surprises. By Friday I want to confirm the representative reruns are stable and that the artifact package is in a shape I can polish quickly.
turns.utterance: Let's set an internal checkpoint for Friday. I'd like to see the baseline reruns and a working artifact draft then, and we can do final polishing over the weekend.
